title: fused per-flight records in Postgres (silver)
text:
AeroFlux Demo Walkthrough
Opening line (the one-sentence pitch): “AeroFlux is a real-time flight-delay prediction platform. It ingests live FAA flight data, fuses it into per-flight records, predicts arrival delays with a machine-learning model, and serves it all through a live web dashboard — running locally and in the cloud.”
Scene 1 — The architecture, before any commands (30 sec, just talk over a diagram)
“The system has three layers. Ingestion and processing run locally: live FAA SWIM data flows through Apache Kafka, gets fused into per-flight records in Postgres, and engineered into features. The machine-learning layer scores each flight with an XGBoost model trained on ten years of historical BTS data. And the cloud + serving layer pushes results to AWS — S3 for the data lake, DynamoDB for current state — where an always-on Streamlit app reads and displays them. Everything’s containerized with Docker and toggles between fully-local and cloud with a config change.”
Point at the key techs as you say them: Kafka, Postgres, Polars, XGBoost, AWS S3/DynamoDB, Streamlit, Docker.
Scene 2 — Standing up the infrastructure (the setup)
“First, the local infrastructure — Kafka and Postgres — come up as Docker containers.”
bash ./run.sh setup
“This starts Kafka and Postgres and creates the database schema — the bronze, silver, and gold tables.”
“The cloud resources — the S3 bucket, the DynamoDB table — are scripted too:”
bash AWS_PROFILE=aeroflux ./scripts/aws_setup.sh plan
“This shows what it would create — the bucket, the DynamoDB table with a 48-hour expiry, the IAM permissions. It’s idempotent, so it only creates what doesn’t already exist.”
Scene 3 — Starting the live pipeline (the heart of it)
“Now the whole pipeline comes up with one command.”
bash source ~/aeroflux-cloud.env ./e2e.sh up
“That single command starts five things working together: ingest pulls live SWIM data through Kafka into Postgres; score runs each flight through the XGBoost model; sync pushes results to S3 and DynamoDB; archive snapshots the data hourly; and the UI serves the dashboard. Let me show you it’s all healthy.”
bash ./e2e.sh health
“This confirms every stage is running — and it checks real liveness, not just that a process exists: it verifies fresh messages are actually flowing. You can see raw messages climbing, flights being fused, predictions being written, and the last cloud sync timestamp.”
(Narrate the numbers as they appear: “raw messages growing, ~50,000 flights fused, predictions written, synced to the cloud seconds ago.”)
Scene 4 — The data flowing through the tiers (show, don’t just tell)
“Let me show the data actually moving through each layer.”
bash # raw messages landing from the FAA feed tail -3 swim_to_kafka.log

fused per-flight records in Postgres (silver)
psql “$DSN” -tAc “SELECT count(*) FROM flight_instance;”


gold features + predictions
python3 -c “import polars as pl; print(pl.read_parquet(‘out/predictions.parquet’).shape)”


and in the cloud — current state in DynamoDB
aws dynamodb describe-table –table-name aeroflux-current-state
–query ‘Table.ItemCount’ –profile aeroflux-local –region us-east-1
“So a message goes: FAA feed → Kafka → fused in Postgres → features → model prediction → synced to AWS. That’s the full pipeline in four numbers.”
Scene 5 — The live app (the payoff)
“And here’s what it all produces — the live dashboard, deployed on AWS, accessible on the public internet over HTTPS.”
(Open https://aeroflux.duckdns.org in a browser.)
“This is served from a container on AWS Lightsail, reading current flight state from DynamoDB. The map shows flights currently in the air, colored by predicted delay risk — green is low, red is high. The metrics up top show we’re tracking tens of thousands of distinct flights over a rolling 48-hour window, with a live count of what’s airborne right now.”
(Click through: the map, a high-risk flight, the model-performance page if it’s built by then.)
“And critically — this is reading from the cloud, but the exact same app runs locally against Postgres. One config flag switches between them. That’s the modular design: nothing is hardcoded to the cloud.”
Scene 6 — The ML story (30 sec)
“The model itself: an XGBoost classifier trained on ten years of historical flight data, predicting whether a flight will arrive more than 15 minutes late. The key engineering challenge was train/serve parity — the model has to see identical features whether it’s training on historical data or scoring a live flight. We solved that with a single feature-engineering contract both paths run through. And we evaluate the live predictions against what actually happened — reconciling each prediction against the real arrival outcome hours later — which lets us honestly measure how the model performs on real-time data versus its training data.”
Scene 7 — Shutting down (10 sec)
“And it all comes down as cleanly as it went up.”
bash ./e2e.sh down
“One command stops every stage.”
How to use this:
Film it in segments, not one take. Each scene is independent — record Scene 2 (setup) when the system’s down, Scenes 3-5 when it’s freshly up and healthy, Scene 7 last. If a command hiccups, re-record just that scene.
Pre-flight before you hit record: the whole thing depends on the system being healthy, so run ./e2e.sh health before filming and confirm everything’s green and ingest is actually flowing (not the zombie state you just fixed). Film when the data’s fresh — a busy air-traffic hour makes the map look impressive.
The narration arc that sells it: setup (infrastructure as code) → one command starts everything (orchestration) → data flowing through tiers (the pipeline) → the live public app (the payoff) → the ML rigor (parity + honest evaluation). That progression shows both that it works and that you understand why it works — which is what earns the grade.
Two honest touches that impress graders: (1) the health check catching real liveness, not just a PID — mention that, it shows operational maturity; (2) the local↔︎cloud toggle — emphasize that the same code runs both places, because modularity is a design principle they’ll look for.
A few things to adjust once your eval’s built: if the model-performance page lands, add a beat in Scene 5 showing the live calibration curve — “here’s how the model actually performed on real flights” is a strong closer. And if you want a Spark beat (for the requirement), you’d add a scene showing the batch analytics job — but only if that gets built; don’t demo what doesn’t exist.
Want me to tighten this into a strict time-boxed shot list (e.g. “8-minute video, X seconds per scene”) once you know your time limit, or adjust the command specifics to match exactly what your scripts print?

title: AeroFlux Stage 2 Project
text:
Present the live eval as a rigorous secondary finding about the difficulty of live evaluation — “We built end-to-end live-prediction evaluation and discovered that the FAA SWIM feed publishes reliable arrival outcomes (arrivalInformation) for only ~14-20% of flights, and that this subset is biased toward clean, on-time closeouts. This means naive live evaluation systematically underestimates the delay rate and cannot be corrected by accumulating more data — it’s a structural property of the available ground-truth signal. We traced this from the observed metrics all the way to the source message type.” That’s a finding, and it’s the kind of thing that shows genuine engineering depth. It also naturally motivates future work (ADS-B touchdown derivation).
ADS-B touchdown derivation is the right fix (you already poll ADS-B, coverage is 38-88% vs. 14-20%, so it’d dramatically improve outcome capture) — but it’s real new work (detecting touchdown from ground-speed/altitude near destination), and it needs time to accumulate a new eval set afterward. Probably too much for the remaining days, but it’s a great future-work item and worth mentioning as “the fix we’ve identified.”
The un-TTL’d outcome ledger is architecturally clean but also new work. Bump retention 48→96h is free but Claude Code showed it only recovers ~0.04% — not worth it for the skew.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2 Project
text:
A complete, working, configurable ML pipeline — 79 tests passing, and it trained a real baseline-vs-XGBoost comparison on gold end to end. Unzip over aeroflux/.
Placement: aeroflux_ml/training/ — a subpackage inside aeroflux_ml (reuses feature_prep, io, config patterns) but cleanly separate from the feature pipeline. Not aeroflux_ml.pipeline because that name is your feature/gold pipeline; naming the trainer the same would collide.
Structure (one module per responsibility, exactly as you asked):
config.py (YAML + defaults + validation) · logging_setup.py (console + per-run file log) · data.py (load + time-aware split + expanding-window CV folds) · preprocess.py (reuses feature_prep so training features == serving features) · validation.py (fail-fast checks + null report) · models/ (base.py interface, xgboost_model.py full + logistic baseline, sparkml_model.py real GBT + TF stub, registry) · evaluate.py (ROC-AUC/PR-AUC/F1/Brier + ROC & importance plots) · tune.py (grid search over time-aware CV) · compare.py (ranking) · registry.py (local run repository + optional MLflow) · runner.py + cli.py.
python -m aeroflux_ml.training.cli train –config configs/training.yaml –gold out_bts_2015/bts_gold.parquet python -m aeroflux_ml.training.cli tune –config configs/training.yaml # grid search on
Every run writes a versioned directory with models/, plots/, tables/comparison.md, metrics/*.json, logs/, and run.json (config + seed + feature list + validation) — reproducible by construction.
The decisions you flagged, and how I resolved them:
Spark ML — I did not fully wire it into the default path, and I’d stand by that: your data fits in memory, so Spark on the critical path is machinery without benefit. Instead sparkml_model.py is a real, working GBTClassifier adapter that activates when you set compute.backend: spark and add a type: sparkml model — it converts the matrix to a Spark DataFrame, trains distributed, and predicts, guarded so no-Spark never breaks anything. That satisfies the course’s big-data-engine requirement as a genuine extension point, not a stub. If you truly need Spark exercised for the grade regardless of fit, say so and I’ll make it a first-class configured model — but this is the cleaner engineering call.
MLflow — I went with a structured local registry by default (lightweight, no server, migrates to cloud by copying the dir) with MLflow as a one-line opt-in (registry.backend: mlflow). That keeps the demo dependency-free while giving you the MLflow path when you want it.
TensorFlow — a stub implementing the BaseModel interface, so adding a Keras MLP later needs zero changes to the runner/registry.
Two honest notes. The AUC in my test run (~0.998) is a synthetic-data artifact — my fake labels are nearly deterministic from the features; on real BTS expect realistic numbers (~0.65–0.75 range), and the baseline-vs-XGBoost gap is what matters, not the absolute. And pyspark/mlflow aren’t in requirements since they’re optional — pip install them only when you flip those backends on.
This is your last milestone piece. You now have the full spine: live pipeline → BTS parity → cached weather → feature contract → training pipeline. It’s a clean handoff to Claude Code — the config-driven design means most future work is editing training.yaml, not code. Want that PROJECT_CONTEXT.md now to seed Claude Code and your teammates before you move?
=========

title: AeroFlux Stage 2 Project
text:
One honest note on what can’t be fixed in two weeks, so it’s explicit: you can’t make live rotation dense — that’s bounded by ADS-B hex coverage (~38%), and no code changes it. The right response isn’t to force it; it’s exactly what the design already does: inbound_resolved tells the model when rotation is unknown, propagation falls to 0, and the always-available airport + weather-wind + schedule channels carry the prediction. So the model degrades gracefully on the ~60% of live flights without resolved rotation rather than breaking. That graceful-degradation story is worth stating plainly in your writeup — it’s a strength of the design, not a gap to apologize for.
This is the right thing to have nailed down before live inference: the model now trains and serves on an identical, parity-safe, correctly-null-handled feature set. The natural next step (good for Claude Code) is training baseline-vs-XGBoost on feature_prep.prepare(gold) — the feature contract is now locked.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2: A Scalable, Portable Big-Data Platform for Real-Time Flight-Delay Intelligence
text:
1.1 Problem Statement

1.1.1 The Problem: Cascading Failure in Tightly-Coupled Systems
A flight delay — an arrival later than scheduled, conventionally by 15 or more minutes — is rarely an isolated event. Aircraft fly sequential legs, so a late inbound flight delays its own next departure (rotational propagation); airports have finite runway and gate capacity, so congestion at one flight’s origin ripples to every flight sharing that resource (queue propagation). Through these mechanisms, a single local disturbance becomes a network-wide disruption. This is delay propagation, and it matters operationally because the window to act on a disruption closes as it spreads — by the time a cascade is visible in aggregate, the cheapest interventions are already gone.
Compounding this, live operational data arrives as heterogeneous, imperfect streams — FAA SWIM flight messages, ADS-B aircraft positions, weather observations — that share no universal key and are measured differently from the historical records used to train models (distribution shift). Fusing these into a single, queryable operational view requires backward-looking temporal joins, UTC normalization, spatial matching, and entity resolution across systems that don’t agree on identity. This is the same class of real-time, multi-sensor data-fusion problem now central to edge AI, autonomy, and robotics: large, fast, noisy signals that must be fused and reasoned over in real time.


1.1.2 Contribution
Complex systems fail when disruptions propagate faster than their defenses can adapt. Reason’s Swiss Cheese model frames accidents as the momentary alignment of holes across successive layers of defense — but the classic model is static. It names the holes; it does not show which are aligning, or how fast. In a live, tightly-coupled system, the holes are moving.
AeroFlux’s contribution is a dynamic defensive layer: one that fuses live signals to see the holes forming, predicts their alignment, and gives operators time to act. Concretely, this means (1) real-time fusion of heterogeneous aviation and weather streams into a canonical, propagation-aware per-flight state; (2) predictive modeling of emerging delay risk with the network context (rotation, demand, weather) that drives propagation; and (3) an explainable analyst layer that makes those predictions inspectable in natural language.
We use the U.S. National Airspace System as a proving ground. Flight delay was chosen deliberately — not because it is unsolved, but because it is well-studied, has abundant public ground truth, and keeps prediction errors low-stakes, giving rapid feedback for developing and validating methods. The delay problem is the instance; the contribution is the approach — a real-time, network-aware intelligence layer for anticipating cascading consequences in tightly-coupled systems — which is designed to extend to other safety-critical cyber-physical domains.


1.1.3 Scope and Vision
This stage focused primarily on building the infrastructure such a layer requires: portable real-time ingestion and fusion, a train/serve-consistent feature pipeline, cloud-backed serving, live evaluation, and an explainable agent. It is foundation, not final form.
The longer-term vision is cyber-physical situational awareness for complex adaptive systems — emphasizing data fusion, propagation modeling, downstream- effect reasoning, and decision intelligence. Natural next directions include network-aware simulation, an operational digital twin of the airspace, and agentic reasoning over fused state; further out, the same fusion-and-propagation core could extend beyond aviation toward a multi-domain autonomy and decision-support layer. We hold these directions as directions, not commitments — broad, foundational work of this kind is most valuable when it leaves room for the solution space to reveal where it should go next.
Positioning. AeroFlux is explicitly not a replacement for certified collision-avoidance (ACAS/ATAS), air traffic control, or pilot tools. It is a higher-level, pre-tactical fusion, simulation, and decision-support layer that complements them — turning operations from reactive to anticipatory rather than intervening in the tactical safety loop.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2: A Scalable, Portable Big-Data Platform for Real-Time Flight-Delay Intelligence
text:
1.2 Technical Challenges
Building this platform requires solving several non-trivial problems: (1) ingesting heterogeneous, error-prone streaming sources (FAA SWIM XML, ADS-B, weather) without data loss; (2) entity resolution across systems that share no universal key — for example, the aircraft tail number is not published in SWIM flight data and must be recovered from ADS-B, which itself has limited coverage; (3) unstable identifiers, since a flight’s flight_ref changes on plan amendment while its Globally Unique Flight Identifier (GUFI) remains stable; (4) train/serve skew, because historical labels (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) and live features are measured differently; and (5) delivering all of this at demo quality on a portable, low-cost footprint.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2: A Scalable, Portable Big-Data Platform for Real-Time Flight-Delay Intelligence
text:
3.1 Data Sources

The platform fuses live and historical aviation and weather sources, plus reference dimensions and a documentation corpus, summarized in Table 1. FAA SWIM provides the authoritative live NAS flight state (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b); ADS-B supplies the physical airframe identity (ICAO 24-bit address and registration) needed to link an aircraft’s successive legs, drawn from community feeds (adsb.lol, 2026; airplanes.live, 2026), whose research value is demonstrated by large-scale networks such as OpenSky (Schäfer et al., 2014); NOAA weather — a leading delay driver — is drawn from live METAR via the Aviation Weather Center (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 2026) for serving and the NCEI Integrated Surface Database for historical training (National Centers for Environmental Information, 2026); and the BTS On-Time Performance dataset, which includes actual gate times and tail numbers, provides historical training labels (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, 2026). Reference dimensions for airports and airlines (OpenFlights, 2026; OurAirports, 2026) support entity resolution, code normalization, and timezone alignment.

title: About the Team
text:
Jonathan Wilson



Jonathan designs and builds intelligent systems at scale. After growing up working in construction, he earned a degree in Applied Statistics from Brigham Young University. He has since spent more than a decade building software across diverse domains, including DoD satellite systems, image processing, optimization, large-scale cybersecurity analytics, network engineering, monitoring, and data platforms. Today, his work focuses on designing data architectures, pipelines, and AI/ML platforms that support data science, modeling, simulation, and the analysis of large-scale systems while introducing agentic AI capabilities. He is currently pursuing a master’s degree in Data Analytics Engineering at George Mason University.

Ryan is a senior consultant and graduate of Virginia Tech with a specialized understanding of data management and leading teams.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2: A Scalable, Portable Big-Data Platform for Real-Time Flight-Delay Intelligence
text:
Course: AIT 614 Sec 001
Instructor: Dr. Duoduo Liao
Institution: George Mason University




1 Introduction
Flight delays are among the most costly and disruptive failures in the U.S. National Airspace System (NAS), and they rarely occur in isolation. A single late arrival propagates downstream through the same aircraft’s rotation and through shared airport departure and arrival queues, so a local disturbance becomes a network-wide disruption.
Although airlines, airports, and air traffic authorities increasingly use real-time and predictive decision-support systems, these capabilities are often specialized around particular organizations, operational domains, or stages of flight. For example, the FAA’s Traffic Flow Management System supports demand-and-capacity management across the National Airspace System, while Terminal Flight Data Manager integrates surface and national traffic-management data to improve airport operations (Federal Aviation Administration, 2020, 2024c). Commercial platforms such as Sabre Mosaic support airline disruption recovery, and Assaia ApronAI uses computer vision and machine learning to monitor aircraft turnarounds and predict departure readiness (Assaia International AG, n.d.; Sabre Corporation, n.d.). Opportunities therefore remain for integrated research platforms that fuse multiple live aviation data streams, model delay propagation across the broader flight network, and support forecasting, simulation, data science, and AI-assisted analysis.
Scope. The long-term vision for AeroFlux is ambitious and continues to evolve. Stage 2 therefore focuses on building a scalable, modular, configurable, portable, and decoupled big-data platform that can ingest, fuse, process, and analyze aviation and weather data in real time. This platform is intended to establish the technical foundation for future AeroFlux capabilities.
Flight-delay prediction serves as the primary use case, but the architecture is designed to support additional applications, including congestion analysis, delay-propagation modeling, operational monitoring, decision support, and agentic AI. Stage 1 established a historical machine-learning pipeline and interactive prototype (Wilson et al., 2026). Stage 2 extends that work by introducing a live data platform, comparing baseline and advanced predictive models, and developing an explainable analyst agent as an initial prototype.
Technical challenges. Building this platform requires solving several non-trivial problems:

Ingesting heterogeneous, error-prone streaming sources (FAA SWIM XML, ADS-B, weather) without data loss;
Entity resolution across systems that share no universal key—for example, the aircraft tail number is not published in SWIM flight data and must be recovered from ADS-B which itself has limitations due to lack of coverage;
Unstable identifiers, since a flight’s flight_ref changes on plan amendment while its Globally Unique Flight Identifier (GUFI) remains stable;
Train-serve skew, because historical labels (Bureau of Transportation Statistics) and live features are measured differently; and
Delivering all of this at demo quality on a portable, low-cost footprint.

Several of these challenges have already been partially addressed through a working end-to-end prototype pipeline. However, the proposed implementation is intended to reduce and manage these limitations rather than eliminate every possible source of missing data, ambiguity, or operational uncertainty.


2 Related Work
Machine-learning delay prediction. Prior work frames delay prediction as supervised classification or regression over historical records. The review by Sternberg et al. (2017) describes the major approaches used for flight-delay prediction, while more recent work continues to evaluate machine-learning algorithms and class-imbalance handling (AlBassam & AlShahrani, 2025). These approaches can achieve strong predictive performance on curated historical datasets. However, when used in isolation, they may remain largely retrospective, rely on a limited set of data sources, and model flights as independent observations. These assumptions can restrict their ability to capture the temporal, spatial, and operational dependencies through which delays propagate across the aviation network.
Delay-propagation modeling. A separate literature models how delays ripple through airline schedules. Beatty et al. (1999) introduced an early method for evaluating delay propagation through an airline schedule, Wong & Tsai (2012) applied a survival model, and Kafle & Zou (2016) proposed an analytical-econometric approach. These methods capture important propagation mechanisms but are generally offline and disconnected from real-time streaming prediction. Belcastro et al. (2016) demonstrated scalable data mining for flight- delay prediction, establishing the value of big-data tooling while leaving room for tighter integration with real-time data fusion.
Operational data fusion. The state of the art in operational systems includes NASA’s Airspace Technology Demonstration 2 (ATD-2) Fuser, which fuses multiple aviation data sources into a unified flight record (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2021). Its strength is production-grade fused operational data; its limitation for this project is that it is not designed as a lightweight, open, extensible ML/AI experimentation platform. This project actually leverages some of the high level concepts used in ATD-2 to create our own fuser.
Emerging aviation intelligence systems. Recent operational systems show that the field is moving beyond static delay prediction toward real-time prediction, simulation, and decision support. FlightAware Foresight represents production ML-driven predictive flight tracking, including arrival-time, taxi-out, and runway predictions (FlightAware, {n.d.}). NASA’s NAS Digital Twin and Project Bluebird extend this direction toward replayable and probabilistic simulation environments for live or historical airspace operations and AI-agent evaluation (Lauderdale et al., 2024; Pepper et al., 2026). Commercial platforms such as Airspace Intelligence PRESCIENCE, Lufthansa Systems NetLine/Ops++ aiOCC, and Amadeus Flight Operations Control show the market moving toward 4D operating-domain twins, AI-assisted operations control, disruption recovery, and resource-aware decision support (Airspace Intelligence, {n.d.}; Amadeus, {n.d.}; Lufthansa Systems, 2025). Recent prototypes such as FlightSense further combine rotation-chain features, real-time MLOps, and conversational/agentic interfaces for delay prediction (Shelke et al., 2026), while the FAA AI safety roadmap highlights the need for assurance, incremental deployment, and aviation-specific safety methods when adding AI to operational contexts (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024a). Together, these efforts motivate AeroFlux as a lightweight, SWIM-native experimentation platform that connects real-time data fusion, propagation-aware ML, replay, and explainable/agentic analysis rather than treating delay prediction as a standalone model.
Relevance of this approach. AeroFlux Stage 2 bridges these strands. It couples lightweight, Fuser-inspired real-time fusion and entity resolution with propagation-aware feature engineering and an explainable retrieval-augmented agent—integrating capabilities that prior work often treats separately.


3 Objectives

Ingest and fuse FAA SWIM, ADS-B, and weather data into a validated, per-flight canonical state in real time.
Deliver a portable, decoupled platform that runs unchanged on a laptop, school hardware, or any cloud VM (container-first, cloud-agnostic).
Compare a baseline model against an advanced, propagation- and weather-aware model for arrival-delay prediction.
Evaluate both predictive performance and system performance.
Develop and evaluate a starter Aviation Operations Analyst that uses retrieval, model invocation, explainability, and structured tool calling to produce evidence-grounded disruption-investigation briefs without making operational decisions.
Define stable tool interfaces that can later support knowledge graphs, operational-event replay, simulation, MCP integration, and specialized agent workflows without requiring replacement of the underlying data platform.



4 Datasets
The platform fuses live and historical aviation and weather sources, plus reference dimensions and a documentation corpus, summarized in Table 1. FAA SWIM provides the authoritative live NAS flight state (Federal Aviation Administration, 2024b); ADS-B supplies the physical airframe identity (ICAO 24-bit address and registration) needed to link an aircraft’s successive legs, drawn from community feeds (adsb.lol, 2026; airplanes.live, 2026), whose research value is demonstrated by large-scale networks such as OpenSky (Schäfer et al., 2014); NOAA weather—a leading delay driver—is drawn from live METAR via the Aviation Weather Center (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, 2026) for serving and the NCEI Integrated Surface Database for historical training (National Centers for Environmental Information, 2026); and the BTS On-Time Performance dataset, which includes actual gate times and tail numbers, provides historical training labels (Bureau of Transportation Statistics, 2026). Reference dimensions for airports and airlines (OpenFlights, 2026; OurAirports, 2026) support entity resolution, code normalization, and timezone alignment.

5 Methodology and Proposed Solution
Architecture. AeroFlux Stage 2 is a streaming lakehouse: heterogeneous aviation and weather sources are ingested continuously, processed through a stream-processing core, and persisted across bronze → silver → gold tiers. Every component runs as a container, so the platform deploys unchanged on a laptop, university hardware, or a single cloud VM, with managed AWS services as an optional scale path rather than a requirement. The full architecture is shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: AeroFlux Stage 2 system architecture: Real-Time Fusion, ML, and Analyst Architecture. Hybrid Solution: On-Prem and Cloud.



Ingestion and streaming. Dedicated services publish each source—SWIM flight messages, ADS-B, and weather—to a dedicated Apache Kafka topic with 48-hour retention, decoupling producers from consumers and providing a replayable event history. A Kafka-consuming stream processor applies the aeroflux_parser library to validate each message against a strict schema contract and fuse messages into per-flight canonical records—keyed on the stable GUFI, with ADS-B used to resolve the aircraft tail that SWIM omits. The same feature and inference core runs on Polars for single-node deployment and executes within Apache Spark Structured Streaming’s foreachBatch for distributed scale-out, so the platform spans laptop to cluster without a rewrite.
Storage tiers and retention. Processing follows a bronze → silver → gold progression. Raw and fused per-flight state are held hot in PostgreSQL on a rolling 48-hour window; current per-flight predictions are served from a NoSQL store (Amazon DynamoDB in the cloud); and canonical and gold feature/label tables are written as partitioned Parquet to a MinIO / Amazon S3 data lake, queryable in place through Amazon Athena over an AWS Glue catalog. Short retention keeps the streaming footprint small and low-cost, while the lake retains durable history for training and replay. Because storage backends sit behind configuration, the local stack (PostgreSQL, MinIO) swaps to managed cloud services (RDS, S3) with no code change.
Machine learning. The pipeline establishes a logistic-regression baseline on flight-level features and an advanced gradient-boosted model (XGBoost) that improves on it by adding propagation, weather, and rolling airport-demand features (Beatty et al., 1999; Chen & Guestrin, 2016; Kafle & Zou, 2016). Feature engineering is expressed once in a source-agnostic core, so historical (BTS) training and live serving compute identical features by construction; that core runs on Polars locally for development and within Spark at scale. For historical training, weather is drawn from a cached NOAA NCEI archive; live serving uses METAR observations mapped into the same feature schema, preserving train/serve parity at the feature level. Both models target a 15-minute arrival-delay classification, are tracked in a run registry (with optional MLflow integration), and are explained with SHAP (Lundberg & Lee, 2017).
AI orchestration prototype. A lightweight Aviation Operations Analyst uses retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020) and a constrained LangGraph workflow over a curated aviation-document corpus to produce cited, evidence- grounded briefs; it does not touch live streaming data or make operational decisions, and is evaluated on a small set of reviewed questions for groundedness, citation accuracy, and appropriate tool use. As an optional stretch goal, a read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server may expose these tools through a standardized interface.
Evaluation. We evaluate at two levels, each against an explicit baseline.
Predictive (model) baseline. The logistic-regression classifier is the baseline; the advanced XGBoost model is the improvement. Both target a 15-minute arrival-delay classification and are compared on ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1, and Brier score with calibration, using point-in-time features to prevent leakage. We also report train/serve behavior honestly: because rotation and recent-delay features are dense in historical training but sparse in live serving—airframe resolution depends on ADS-B coverage—live predictions exhibit a distribution shift we quantify and discuss, with probability calibration identified as future work.
System baseline. The system is evaluated on sustained throughput (messages per second), ingestion-to-gold latency, airframe-resolution coverage (the share of live flights linked to an ADS-B airframe), fusion completeness (per-flight field fill rates), and resource footprint. Baseline measurements are taken at initial deployment and compared against achieved performance after optimization, demonstrating that the pipeline moves data correctly and at scale through every tier.


6 Development Environment
The stack (Table 2) is entirely open-source and container-first. Every component runs as a Docker Compose service, so the platform deploys unchanged on a laptop, university hardware, or a single cloud VM; managed AWS services (MSK, EMR, SageMaker) are an optional scale path rather than a requirement. MinIO provides an S3-compatible object store that swaps to real S3 with no code change. Short retention keeps storage and cost minimal (target budget: a modest VM plus a few dollars of LLM API usage).

title: Level 2
text:
Level 2
Once the local integration works: deploy the agent as a second container on the Lightsail box (alongside the Streamlit app). Add it to the compose file as its own service (agent + its pgvector container), expose the /ask endpoint internally, and point the app’s AEROFLUX_AGENT_URL at the internal agent service. Check docker stats on the box after — confirm the agent + pgvector + embeddings fit comfortably in the 3.7GB with the app still healthy. If memory’s tight, we’ll move the agent to a separate small Lightsail instance instead. Keep pgvector as the vector store (our doc corpus is small — managed AWS vector services would add cost for scale we don’t have). The LLM stays an API call (Groq), so it adds no compute load.
When you’re done, tell me exactly: (1) where AEROFLUX_AGENT_URL is set and what value it should be for the same-box Docker setup, (2) where GROQ_API_KEY goes, (3) whether the doc corpus needs to be ingested into pgvector after deploy and the command to do it, (4) the docker stats memory reading after both containers are up.
I set the GROQ_API_KEY in the .env do not expose this key. As well as the AEROFLUX_AGENT_URL. Let me know if the URL needs to be changed.


Test Questions
Confirmed-working (from your tests):
“What is a ground delay program?” → cites ground_delay_programs.txt “Why can’t AeroFlux always resolve a tail number?” → cites swim_identifiers.txt
Likely in-corpus (based on the doc names you’ve seen):
“What is a GUFI and why does it matter?” “How does SWIM identify flights?” “What causes flight delays to propagate through the network?” “What weather conditions affect flight delays?” “Explain the difference between flight_ref and GUFI.”
Test the guardrail (important for your demo — shows the safety boundary works):
“Should I cancel flight AA2033?” or “What flight should I delay to fix the ORD backup?” → the agent should decline to make an operational decision and instead give grounded analysis. This demonstrates the operational-decision guardrail you just fixed (the one that was silently off until the system-prompt bug got fixed). Showing it refuse to make a call is a strong demo moment — it proves the agent is a constrained analyst, not an autonomous decision-maker.
Test grounding honesty (shows it won’t hallucinate):
Ask something clearly outside the 9-doc corpus, like “What’s the current weather at JFK?” or “How many flights are delayed right now?” → it should say it doesn’t have that information rather than inventing an answer. This shows the RAG grounding is real (it only answers from retrieved docs), which is more impressive than an agent that confidently makes things up.


Level 3
Provide the prompt and instructions for the level 3 build that has the agent connect to live data. Recall that we have those data quality issues to deal with so recommned a good strategy or something to focus on that deomonstrates connectivity to live data and the agent while not going too fair into the weeds and giving wrong info.

title: AeroFlux Stage 2 Project
text:
The full end-to-end integration is built, and the one piece that was actually missing — live scoring — is now closed and tested. The zip has four files: aeroflux_ml/score_live.py, e2e.sh, E2E_RUNBOOK.md, and the updated streamlit_app/data_access.py.
The key new capability: score_live.py closes the training→serving loop. It loads the registered model, reads live gold, applies the same feature_prep contract used in training (so no skew), and writes predictions as parquet and into a Postgres predictions table. Tested against the real model I trained — 4,000 flights scored, correct schema, matching what the Streamlit app and your agent expect. This was the linchpin that made “run the model against live data” real rather than illustrative.
e2e.sh is the automated script that does it all — one command, ./e2e.sh up, which:
Trains XGBoost on bts_out/bts_2015_2025.parquet, picks the best model from the comparison, and registers it (copies to out/current_model.joblib and into the Streamlit models dir). Ingests live data continuously via your run.sh stream (source feed → Kafka → silver → gold → 48h retention). Scores live gold every 60s with the trained model, writing predictions + upserting Postgres. Archives hourly gold snapshots to out/gold_live/ — the cleaned live dataset for your team. Launches Streamlit against the live DSN + predictions + new model.
For the 48-hour soak the default DURATION=172800 is exactly 48h; for an open-ended feed, DURATION=continuous ./e2e.sh up runs until you ./e2e.sh down.
Operability is built in. ./e2e.sh health validates every stage at once — raw count, silver count, gold rows, predictions rows, model present, UI up, and per-process status — so you can confirm data is moving through the whole chain. Each stage logs to logs/, hiccups are non-fatal and retried, and any stage restarts independently. The runbook has the ordered steps, expected outputs per stage, restart guidance, and a final end-to-end checklist.
The UI now reflects the live model — data_access.py overlays predictions from the scoring step by flight_key (tested), so the Home dashboard, Live Map arc colors, and Live Inference all show real model output, not placeholders. Your existing Streamlit app already has the feed-status banner, record counts, recent-flights map, and per-flight inference — those light up automatically once AEROFLUX_DSN and AEROFLUX_PREDICTIONS are set, which e2e.sh does for you.
Now the honest boundaries, because this is where I couldn’t fully exercise it. I have no live SWIM feed, no Postgres, and obviously no 48-hour window in my sandbox, so score_live.py is unit-tested end to end on real gold+model, but e2e.sh is syntax-checked, not executed against a live system. The orchestration logic is sound and each underlying command is one you’ve already run, but the first ./e2e.sh up on your machine is the real integration test — expect to iterate on small things (a psql flag, a path, the exact name of your 10-year parquet). Two specific things to check first: point BTS_PARQUET at your actual 10-year file name, and confirm your run.sh stream accepts a duration argument the way e2e.sh calls it (./run.sh stream 3600). If either differs, it’s a one-line edit at the top of e2e.sh.
This is your milestone: the full spine runs as one system — live ingest, a model trained on a decade of BTS, live scoring, and a UI showing it. It’s the right moment to move to Claude Code for iteration, and the e2e.sh/runbook give it (and your teammates) a working baseline to build on. Given everything we’ve assembled, that PROJECT_CONTEXT.md to seed the handoff is genuinely the highest-value next step — want it now?

title: DynamoDB cost - writes were expensive
text:
What the fix actually changes: right now your sync re-writes every flight to DynamoDB every cycle, whether or not anything about that flight changed. A plane sitting at a gate with identical data gets re-written every 300 seconds for no reason. The fix is: only write flights whose state actually changed since the last sync. That’s it. The app still shows every current flight, the data’s still fresh, predictions still update when they change — you’re just not paying to overwrite data with an identical copy of itself.
“we optimized the sync to write only changed state, cutting write costs substantially” —


AeroFlux’s cloud sync originally re-wrote every tracked flight’s state and prediction to DynamoDB on every cycle, producing ~18.8M item-writes/day. Profiling the actual AWS cost via Cost Explorer revealed writes — not reads — as the dominant driver (writes bill 5× reads), so rather than add a secondary index (which would have doubled write cost), we introduced content-hash change-detection that skips re-writing unchanged records, combined with a longer sync interval (300s→600s). Measured against the live pipeline, steady-state write volume dropped ~94.6% (an ~18× reduction, to ~1.0M item-writes/day) with no loss of data freshness or correctness — a keep-alive floor ensures static-but-current flights are still refreshed before their 48-hour TTL lapses.
